title: Measure the leak, apply the laws, design for real conditions

say: Measure the leak, apply the laws, and design for real conditions.
This is the video for module one of UX Design Fundamentals: outcomes, cognition and context.
User experience, or UX, is everything a person goes through to get something done with a product. UI, the user interface, is only the part you see and touch.

say: Clients will not pay for better UX as an opinion. They pay for a change in a number they care about, like more completed sign-ups or fewer support calls.

say: A funnel lists the steps users pass through to reach a goal, with how many reach each step.
For example, Amaka is hired by a Lagos savings app. She asks for last month's numbers instead of opinions. 10,000 people downloaded the app.

panel.heading: Read a funnel to find the leak
items: Downloads: 10,000
Started sign-up: 6,200 (62%)
Passed BVN check: 3,100 (50%)
Funded wallet: 2,480 (80%)

say: 6,200 started sign-up. Step conversion is people at a step divided by people at the step before, so that is 62%.

say: Only 3,100 passed the BVN check, which is the Bank Verification Number. That step loses half of everyone who reaches it.

say: 2,480 funded their wallet, which is 80% of those who passed. So the BVN step, at 50%, is the leak, and the best place to research first.

say: But numbers only show where people leave, never why. Always pair a funnel with interviews or usability tests before you redesign anything.

panel.rule: Numbers show where people leave. Research shows why.

say: Hick's law says the more equal choices you show, the slower people decide. A home screen with 18 equal tiles slows people down. Group options, and put the most common tasks first.

panel.heading: Three laws you will quote often

cards.d: More equal choices means slower decisions. Group options and put the two or three common tasks first.
Far and small is slow. Near and large is fast. Put key buttons big and close to the thumb.
Users expect your product to work like the others they use. Follow conventions unless innovation adds value.

say: Fitts's law says the time to reach a target depends on its distance and size. For example, Zainab recommends a full-width Pay now bar fixed near the bottom, where the thumb already rests.
On phones, make targets 44 to 48 pixels, and never below 24.

say: Jakob's law says users spend most of their time on other products. If every bank app they know puts Transfer on the home screen, do not hide yours in a menu.

say: Working memory is small. So do not make people remember things the interface could show them.

panel.heading: Recognition beats recall
left: Remember a code from last screen

say: Let them pick from recent beneficiaries, show the code again, and offer search with suggestions.
Chunk long numbers too, and show the account name so people confirm by recognition.

say: Every megabyte is paid for by the user. For example, Tunde's farm price page was 4 megabytes, opened 5 times a day. That is 600 megabytes a month. He set a budget of 800 kilobytes, cutting it to 120.

panel.heading: Design for the conditions users live in
items: Costly data: set a performance budget
Network drops: save progress locally
Feature phones: USSD or SMS for core task
Shared phones: quick logout, PIN, private alerts
Many languages: native-speaker review

say: When the network drops, long forms should keep what was typed, and offline, failed and pending states must look different.

say: For people without internet, offer USSD, the star code hash menus that work on any GSM phone.

say: Phones are often shared, so offer quick logout and never show balances on notifications. And offer the languages your users speak, checked by native speakers.

say: USSD has no images and sessions time out quickly. Put the most common task as option 1, and keep each screen under about 160 characters to be safe across networks.

panel.heading: Five rules for a USSD menu
items: Most common task is option 1
Keep each screen under about 160 characters
0 Back and 00 Main menu on every screen
Confirm amount and recipient before PIN
Send an SMS receipt

say: Use 0 for Back and 00 for Main menu, the same way on every screen.

panel.heading: Five rules for a USSD menu
items: Most common task is option 1
Keep each screen under about 160 characters
0 Back and 00 Main menu on every screen
Confirm amount and recipient before PIN
Send an SMS receipt

say: Show the amount and the recipient's name before asking for a PIN. Then send an SMS receipt, because the session closes and users cannot scroll back.

panel.rule: Confirm amount and name before the PIN. Send an SMS receipt.

say: Payments need extra care. After a timeout, show We are checking your payment, with the real status from the server, never a try again button that may charge twice.
Always show a transaction reference and official support channels inside the product. Worried users who search online for customer care numbers can meet fraudsters.

panel.heading: Payment states users can trust
items: After a timeout, check, don't retry
Show the real status from the server
Always show a transaction reference
Show official support channels in the app

say: To remember. Find the step with the lowest conversion first, then research why people leave. Make key targets big and close. Design for recognition.
And treat data cost, network drops and shared phones as part of the experience.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Fix the step with the lowest conversion first
Analytics show where; research shows why
Big, close targets: 44 to 48 px on phones
Design for recognition, not recall
Data cost, offline and shared phones are UX
